b6_6_context.printed: The Confederacy fielded about 16 sharpshooter battalions drawn from regiments; dress was butternut or gray with slouch hats and a mix of issue, civilian and captured clothing. The Enfield P1853 was the most common prized rifle; also the Enfield musketoon, the Whitworth (.451, hexagonal bore, 36 or 39 in barrels; 100-500 bought; about $1,000 per cased Whitworth with 1,000 rounds, scope about $200 extra) and the Kerr .442; one division got 30 Whitworths and 16 Kerrs ([AR-Sharpshooting], which does not name Georgia or Alabama units). A popular article gives the Whitworth effective range as about 2,000 yd; this is overstated (Wikipedia gives 800-1,000 yd). Low reliability ([WeAreMighty]). Whitworth cannons versus Whitworth rifles: the Oak Hill marker, via a forum transcription (weak), lists "Two Whitworths, Two 3 Inch Rifles" in Hardaway's Alabama battery (Hurt's), McIntosh's battalion, on Oak Hill on July 3. The notes infer this is the breech-loading Whitworth cannon, not the sharpshooter rifle; the sources conflate the two.

b6_6_context.printed: The Sharps .52 breechloader, about 30 in barrel, double-set triggers on many, sights to 700-800 yd, about 2,000 supplied; Berdan feuded with Chief of Ordnance Ripley; Colt 1855 revolving rifles were issued first and replaced by Sharps in 1862 (issued from May 1862 per Wikipedia) ([AR-Sharpshooting], [Wiki-1USS]). Wikipedia puts accuracy at about 600 yd and claims 8-10 rounds a minute. Private target rifles with Malcolm or Morgan James scopes (.36-.45 caliber, up to about 25 lb) were common but Berdan found them impractical; Truman Head ("California Joe") carried a scoped rifle of about 32 lb ([AR-Sharpshooting]). Heavy target rifles were kept in wagons, one per company; the two regiments used Sharps rifles ([AR-Guns]). Whether the men still carried Sharps in July 1863 is stated by most sources but is not directly confirmed for that month in the notes.

drill.printed: Loading a muzzle-loader was a nine-step drill, against five for breech-loaders ([ABT-SmallArms]). The step-by-step list is not in the research notes. Leads to verify from Casey's Infantry Tactics (1862) and Hardee's Rifle and Light Infantry Tactics: the standard nine commands are, from memory, load; handle cartridge; tear cartridge; charge cartridge; draw rammer; ram cartridge; return rammer; prime; shoulder arms. This is unverified memory and must be checked before an animation set is built. The drill is the basis of the loading animation; the Hardee vs Casey drill differences are open.

ballistic_modelling_rule.printed: Ballistic modelling rule (inferred): derive each gun's range curve from the published 5-degree range plus the 3-inch rifle's 16-degree maximum of about 4,180 yd. Smoothbores fall well behind rifles beyond about 1,500 yd, so Napoleons on July 3 had to be forward or near the crest to reach Seminary Ridge (1,400 yd or more) with shell or case. The Whitworth and Blakely breechloaders are modelled as long-range, flat-trajectory rifles; their July 3 effect from Oak Hill rests on a forum claim, not an official source. Per-elevation range tables are an open gap (see end of section).

fuzes.printed: Fuzes: - Timed (paper or wooden) fuze: the cutter trims the fuze to range before loading; the flame from the main charge ignites it. Described as the most problematic type (Civil War News, The Artillery Fuze). Example Confederate paper fuze: C.S. Laboratory Richmond, May 1864, about 4 seconds per inch, wrapped in wax paper (a May 1864 example, not July 1863; tier: documented but date-shifted). - Percussion fuzes: plunger-and-anvil, explode on impact; used with rifled shell. Union 3-inch ammunition on hand in Wheeler's 13th NY on July 2 was percussion and canister only (13th NY Battery site). - Confederate reliability: a Confederate officer's report of December 1863 stated many fuzes exploded early and about half of friction primers failed; Union primers and fuzes failed less (Civil War News). A Richmond (Brown's Island) laboratory explosion shut the arsenal temporarily: March 1863 (Civil War News) versus April 1863 (History Is Now Magazine) - date conflict. - July 3 specifics (secondary blog, History Is Now): fuzes burned longer than expected; replacements from Selma and Charleston burned about one second longer than Richmond-made fuzes; later tests suggested bursts 150-200 yd farther back than intended; one officer blamed softened resin filler mixing with powder in humid weather. The American Battlefield Trust says many shells with defective fuzes fell short or flew over. Both short and long attested; the dominant claim in the blog is long. - Not found: Bormann fuze, Schenkl and Hotchkiss specifics; which percussion fuze models each side used at Gettysburg (open gap).

crew.printed_sequence: Documented sequence (NPS Fort Scott artillery drill page, a Union-pattern light-artillery demonstration): commands are commence firing, load, ready, fire, cease firing. No. 1 sponges while No. 3 thumbs the vent; No. 2 takes the round from No. 5 and puts it in the muzzle; No. 1 rams; the gunner sights; No. 3 moves the trail with the trailspike on the gunner's direction; No. 5 fetches the next round from Nos. 6 and 7 at the limber (No. 6 cuts the fuzes); the gunner steps clear and calls ready; No. 3 pricks the cartridge through the vent; No. 4 hooks the friction primer to the lanyard, inserts it and pulls the lanyard taut on "Fire"; after firing the piece is run back up. CVBT adds: No. 2 also uses the worm staff after firing; No. 6 tends the chest; No. 7 hands rounds; spare men handle horses; the prolonge is a long rope on the trail used to move the piece without hitching up.

crew_size.printed: Crew-size conflict (8 versus 9) and how the engine handles it: NPS Fort Scott counts nine (gunner, chief of caisson, Nos. 1-7); CVBT counts roughly eight (gunner plus seven numbered); Wikipedia states eight crew plus four men for horses and equipment but also gives nine cannoneers in the Napoleon article; the horse-artillery page gives a typical crew of nine. The two counts disagree only on whether the chief of caisson belongs in the detachment. Engine rule (inferred, so tier: inferred): the working detachment at the piece is the gunner plus Nos. 1-7, which is eight men and common to every source; the chief of caisson is a ninth soldier stationed with the limber/caisson line, not at the piece. A battery's detachment size is then a parameter (8 default, 9 including chief of caisson) that can be changed without redoing animation, because the chief of caisson has no gun-side state. When casualties reduce a crew, the drill degrades by dropping roles in this order (plausible-procedural, seeded): spare hands and No. 7 first, then No. 6 and No. 5 merge, then No. 2 and No. 4 pair up, with the gunner always last. Confederate crew size is an open gap (often smaller crews, no source retrieved).
